If you only need a summary, an aggregatable function is dramatically cheaper than collecting all values.

followUps.question: How does reduceByKey relate to this in the RDD world?
followUps.answer: In the RDD API, reduceByKey performs map-side combining before the shuffle, like a partial aggregation, while groupByKey shuffles all values first and is much slower. In the DataFrame API, Catalyst applies the same partial-aggregation optimization automatically for aggregatable functions, so you usually get the efficient behavior without choosing it explicitly.

followUps.question: When would you repartition before a groupBy?
followUps.answer: If the input has very few partitions, the pre-aggregation runs with little parallelism and the stage is slow before the shuffle even happens. Repartitioning up front, or simply ensuring enough shuffle partitions for the aggregation stage, gives the work enough parallelism. I avoid repartitioning by the exact grouping key unnecessarily, though, since the groupBy already triggers the needed shuffle.

question: Your job uses the default 200 shuffle partitions. On a tiny dataset it makes hundreds of empty tasks, and on a huge dataset each partition is gigabytes and spills. How do you set the right partition count?
directAnswer: 200 is just a default and rarely matches your data. The right count comes from the shuffle data size divided by a target per-partition size of around 100 to 200MB. Better still, I enable Adaptive Query Execution, which coalesces or splits shuffle partitions at runtime based on actual sizes, so I do not have to hardcode a number that is wrong for some inputs.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: spark.sql.shuffle.partitions controls how many partitions result from a shuffle like a join or aggregation, defaulting to 200. This single static number applies regardless of whether the data is megabytes or terabytes, which is why it is so often wrong.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Spark needs some default for post-shuffle parallelism, and 200 was a historical compromise. The problem is that the ideal count depends on data size and cluster cores, which vary per job and per run, so a fixed default is too many partitions for small data and far too few for large data.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Diagnose: check the shuffle write size of the stage and divide by your target per-partition size to see how far 200 is from ideal, and watch for empty tasks on small data or spill on large data. Options: set shuffle partitions manually to total shuffle size divided by roughly 128MB; or enable AQE so Spark coalesces small partitions and splits large ones based on runtime statistics. Decision: prefer AQE because it adapts per run and per stage automatically, and fall back to manual tuning for predictable workloads or when AQE is unavailable.

whyImportant: The 200-partition default is one of the most common reasons Spark jobs are slower than they should be, in both directions, and many engineers never touch it. Knowing both the manual sizing rule and the AQE solution is bread-and-butter tuning knowledge that interviewers expect.
realWorldExample: A pipeline ran the same code on small reference tables and on the main fact table. The 200 default created hundreds of empty tasks on the small tables and gigabyte spilling partitions on the fact table. Enabling AQE let Spark coalesce to a handful of partitions for the small data and expand for the large data, fixing both extremes without per-job tuning.

nestedTopics.title: Target partition size
nestedTopics.explanation: A widely used target is roughly 100 to 200MB of data per shuffle partition, which keeps each task's working set in memory while giving enough tasks for parallelism. Dividing total shuffle size by this target gives a sensible static partition count.

nestedTopics.title: AQE coalescing and splitting
nestedTopics.explanation: Adaptive Query Execution reads the actual sizes of shuffle output at runtime and merges tiny partitions together and splits oversized ones, so the final partition count fits the real data. This removes most of the need to guess the right static number.

nestedTopics.title: Empty tasks overhead
nestedTopics.explanation: When there are far more partitions than data, many tasks have little or no data but still carry scheduling and startup overhead. Hundreds of near-empty tasks add latency with no benefit, which is the small-data failure mode of a too-high partition count.

followUps.question: Does AQE make manual shuffle partition tuning obsolete?
followUps.answer: Mostly, but not entirely. AQE handles the common cases of coalescing small partitions and splitting skewed ones very well, so for many jobs you can stop hardcoding the number. For highly predictable, performance-critical workloads, or environments where AQE is off, a tuned static value still has value, and understanding the manual rule helps you sanity-check what AQE is doing.

followUps.question: How does shuffle partition count interact with output file count?
followUps.answer: The final shuffle partition count typically determines how many files a write produces, one per partition per output path. So a too-high count contributes to the small files problem, while a too-low count can make giant files. Tuning shuffle partitions or coalescing before the write lets you control both task parallelism and resulting file sizes together.

followUps.question: Is 200 ever actually the right number?
followUps.answer: Only by coincidence, when the shuffle data size happens to be around 200 times your target partition size and the cluster has matching parallelism. For a moderate dataset of maybe 25 to 40GB it can be roughly right, but treating 200 as a deliberate choice rather than an unexamined default is what matters, and AQE removes the need to land on it exactly.

question: Reading a single huge CSV file into Spark is extremely slow and uses only one or two tasks. Why, and how do you make ingestion faster?
directAnswer: A single CSV, especially if gzip-compressed, often cannot be split, so Spark reads it with one task no matter how big it is, and CSV itself is row-based and schema-inferred, which is slow. I speed it up by providing an explicit schema to skip inference, splitting the input into multiple files for parallel reads, and ideally converting to a columnar format like Parquet for any repeated reads.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: CSV ingestion in Spark involves splitting the input into partitions, parsing text rows, and applying a schema. Performance depends on whether the file can be split for parallel reading, whether the schema is inferred by scanning the data, and the inherent cost of text parsing.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: CSV is a row-oriented text format with no built-in schema or block structure, so Spark must parse every character and, by default, scan the data to infer types. Compressed single files like gzip are not splittable, so all of that work falls to a single task, which caps parallelism.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Diagnose: check how many tasks the read uses, and if it is one or two on a large file, suspect non-splittable compression or a single file; check whether schema inference is doing an extra pass. Options: supply an explicit schema so Spark skips the inference scan; split the source into many files or use a splittable compression so multiple tasks read in parallel; and convert to Parquet so future reads are columnar, compressed, and splittable with pushdown. Decision: for a one-time read, at least set an explicit schema and split the file; for repeated reads, convert to Parquet once and read that thereafter.

whyImportant: Slow CSV ingestion is a common real bottleneck at the start of pipelines, and the non-splittable-single-file trap surprises many engineers. Knowing why CSV is slow and that columnar formats and explicit schemas fix it is practical knowledge that interviewers expect for data ingestion.
realWorldExample: A nightly load read a 30GB gzip CSV that took 40 minutes on a single task because gzip is not splittable. The team had the upstream system emit Parquet instead, and the same load became a parallel, columnar read across the cluster that finished in a few minutes, with the added benefit of column pruning for downstream queries.

nestedTopics.title: Splittable vs non-splittable formats
nestedTopics.explanation: Spark can read a splittable file with many parallel tasks, each handling a block. Gzip CSV is not splittable so it is read by one task, while formats like Parquet, or CSV compressed with splittable codecs, allow parallel reads across the cluster.

nestedTopics.title: Schema inference cost
nestedTopics.explanation: Without an explicit schema, Spark scans the CSV to infer column types, which is an extra full pass over the data. Providing a StructType schema skips that scan entirely, both speeding the read and avoiding incorrect type guesses.

nestedTopics.title: Columnar formats and pushdown
nestedTopics.explanation: Parquet stores data by column with embedded statistics, enabling Spark to read only needed columns and skip row groups that fail a filter. Converting CSV to Parquet once makes every subsequent read faster and cheaper than re-parsing text.

followUps.question: If you must keep CSV, what is the single biggest win?
followUps.answer: Making the input splittable so the read parallelizes, either by having the source emit many smaller files instead of one giant file, or by using a splittable compression codec rather than gzip. After that, supplying an explicit schema avoids the inference pass. Those two changes alone turn a single-task crawl into a parallel read across the cluster.

followUps.question: Why is Parquet so much faster to read than CSV?
followUps.answer: Parquet is binary and columnar, so Spark reads only the columns a query needs instead of parsing every field of every row, and it carries statistics that let Spark skip whole chunks that cannot match a filter. It is also compressed efficiently and splittable. CSV forces a full text parse of everything regardless of what the query needs, which is fundamentally more work.

followUps.question: How do you handle the conversion if the source can only produce CSV?
followUps.answer: I run a one-time or scheduled conversion job that reads the CSV with an explicit schema and writes Parquet partitioned sensibly, then point downstream jobs at the Parquet. The conversion pays the CSV parsing cost once, and every consumer afterward benefits from the faster columnar reads, so it amortizes quickly when the data is read more than once.

question: A stage is 99 percent done but hangs for a long time on the final one or two tasks. This straggler is killing your job's tail latency. How do you diagnose and mitigate it?
directAnswer: A straggler is one or two tasks that take far longer than the rest, and the stage cannot finish until they do. The usual causes are data skew putting more data in that partition, or a slow or failing node hosting that task. I check the UI to see whether the straggler has more input than its peers, which means skew, or similar input but slow execution, which means a bad node, and I enable speculative execution for node-related stragglers.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A straggler is a task that runs dramatically longer than the others in its stage, so the stage's completion is gated on it. Because a stage only finishes when its last task does, a single straggler can dominate the stage's wall-clock time.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Stragglers arise either from skew, where that task simply has more data to process, or from environmental causes, where a slow disk, a noisy neighbor, or a degrading node makes an otherwise normal task crawl. Distinguishing the two is the key to the right fix.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Diagnose: in the stage's task table, sort by duration and inspect the straggler's input size and shuffle read versus the median; much larger input means skew, while similar input but long duration points to a slow node. Options: for skew, apply salting or AQE skew handling so no single partition is huge; for node issues, enable speculative execution so Spark launches a duplicate of a slow task on another node and takes whichever finishes first; and check executor logs for the slow node's health. Decision: fix the data with skew handling when input is uneven, and use speculation when input is even but a node is slow, since speculation cannot help true skew.

whyImportant: Stragglers are a direct hit to tail latency and SLA, and they are confusing because the job looks almost done. Knowing the skew-versus-slow-node split and that speculative execution helps one but not the other demonstrates a mature understanding of distributed execution.
realWorldExample: A join stage routinely hung on its last task. The UI showed that task had the same input size as the others but ran on an executor whose node had a failing disk, so it was just slow. Enabling speculative execution let Spark relaunch that task on a healthy node and finish it quickly, cutting the stage's tail latency substantially while the team replaced the bad node.

nestedTopics.title: Speculative execution
nestedTopics.explanation: When a task runs much slower than its peers, Spark can launch a speculative copy on another executor and use whichever finishes first. It is controlled by spark.speculation and helps with slow-node stragglers, but it wastes resources and does not help genuine skew since the duplicate has the same large data.

nestedTopics.title: Skew straggler vs node straggler
nestedTopics.explanation: A skew straggler has much larger input than its peers, so it is slow because it has more work. A node straggler has comparable input but runs slowly due to hardware or contention. The input-size comparison in the UI is what tells them apart and dictates the fix.

nestedTopics.title: Tail latency
nestedTopics.explanation: Tail latency is the time spent waiting on the slowest tasks rather than the average. Because a stage finishes only when its last task does, minimizing the worst-case task, through skew handling or speculation, is what improves the overall job completion time.

followUps.question: Why does speculative execution not help with data skew?
followUps.answer: Speculation relaunches the slow task elsewhere, but if the task is slow because its partition genuinely holds far more data, the duplicate has the exact same large partition and will be just as slow. Speculation only helps when the original is slow due to a bad node, not when the work itself is larger. For skew you must change the data distribution with salting or AQE.

followUps.question: What are the downsides of enabling speculative execution everywhere?
followUps.answer: Speculation launches duplicate tasks, consuming extra cores and potentially doing redundant work, which wastes resources if many tasks are merely a bit slow rather than truly stuck. It can also cause issues with non-idempotent writes if a speculative task and the original both commit. So it is best enabled thoughtfully for workloads prone to node stragglers rather than blindly across all jobs.

followUps.question: How do you confirm it is a bad node rather than skew without guessing?
followUps.answer: I compare the straggler task's input size and shuffle read to the median in the stage's task table. If they are similar but the duration is far higher, the data is balanced and the cause is environmental, so I then check that executor's host and logs for disk, GC, or contention problems. If the input is much larger, it is skew, and node investigation would be a dead end.
